comments.author: Alexsky2
comments.textRawHtml:
For those interested, there was a 2009 outage of the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure that at a surface level seems like it could be a similar failure mode. At the very least, it is an interesting read on how the FAAs systems operate, since a lot of the discussion so far has been wild speculation from people with little knowledge on how the national airspace system actually operates: https://www.oig.dot.gov/library-item/29670

Of particular note is this section: Risks of FTI Outages for Existing Operational Services As of December 2009, Harris reported that there are a total of 20,982 services operating on the FTI network. While FAA has transitioned all 1,808 IP services supporting FAA flight plans to the new FTI fiber optic network, additional risks will be introduced when the Agency begins transitioning other FAA services, such as En Route Automation Modernization (ERAM) and NextGen platforms, which also require IP technology to operate. Moreover, there are 19,174 existing services that may be transitioned to the new FTI fiber optic network. According to FAA, transitioning these remaining services is important because FTI now connects older FAA systems that provide safety-critical voice and surveillance radar information by utilizing Time Division Multiplex (TDM) technology, instead of IP services.

comments.author: AbbeFaria
comments.textRawHtml:
Ex-MSFT here, sharing my outdated POV based on working on a product that was using Microsoft Exchange and therefore was hooked onto the email delivery pipeline.

Note that the infra for M365, Azure etc is different. They would be running on servers hosted in MSFT DCs but have completely different CI/CD pipelines. M365 services have their own deployment pipelines and it takes on the order of weeks to deploy your changes to production.

Considering the fact that Outlook is down, clearly email doesn’t seem to be working. So email uses something called Microsoft Exchange Server, there used to be an on-premises version of this but MS stopped supporting it to run the cloud version hereby called M365. Email is one big “macro-service”, if you’re running Windows Server, look at the process called “EdgeTransport.exe” this is responsible for sending/receiving email on Windows Servers. There are probably multiple 100s of services supported by 100s of teams that are run while email is routed from sender to receiver via MSFT Exchange servers. My recollection is that even if one of these services goes down or introduces latency in the pipeline, it caused a major incident. When I was working in M365 Security in 2024, this Exchange Server pipeline was called “legacy” because it’s one big .NET Framework service. I don’t know if they upgraded to .NET core but developing on this was as HN comments say, very janky.

The reason Teams doesn’t seem to be down is that Teams services are completely different and are written using .NET Core and have their own separate release pipeline. It was much easier to interact with Teams services. I actually worked closely with the team that was responsible for ingesting Teams messages to the customer’s data store. Their code base was much more modern and easy to understand. Exchange Server not so much.

I don’t know if what I said is accurate but know that Exchange server code was like a fossil that didn’t change as much, over the ~5 years I worked on it from 2019-2024.

Story time over.

children.textRawHtml:
> So email uses something called Microsoft Exchange Server, there used to be an on-premises version of this but MS stopped supporting it ...

On-premises Exchange is still supported and licensed. It's a subscription instead of a perpetual license.

> I don’t know if what I said is accurate but know that Exchange server code was like a fossil that didn’t change as much, over the ~5 years I worked on it from 2019-2024.

Exchange is a mature product (albeit not without its flaws). Its era of change was between its 2007 and 2013 versions (inclusive) when it was made more modular and many parts were ported to the .NET runtime. The 2016, 2019, and now Subscription Edition codebases were more of an evolution and has much less churn.

comments.author: Silfen
comments.textRawHtml:
Reading this thread makes me realize that seemingly no one has heard the basic, mundane case for why Nvidia would want to do so much "circular financing" as a matter of totally normal business strategy. This may not be the whole story, but it's worth understanding.

Because of bottlenecks in the supply chain, Nvidia knows it is going to sell 100% of its inventory. They could raise prices quite a bit more, but then their only customers would be hyperscalers (building competing chips) and possibly OpenAI and Anthropic. Nvidia is willing to forgo present day profits for the strategic value of keeping its customer base diverse and promoting the network effects of e.g. CUDA. Instead of quoting a lower price per GPU to neoclouds and startups, they finance purchases of chips, but the two are roughly equivalent (financing means Nvidia takes on more risk, but has more upside and locks in future demand). It is in their commercial interest to have many competing buyers of their chips.

Obviously this creates fun mechanisms for fraud and wacky accounting (and I'm agnostic as to whether that's happening here), but it's worth knowing about the boring/obvious story before donning your tinfoil hat.

Hehehe my pet theory is that Jensen was using exactly the opposite strategy to secure that “avalanche of chips and wafers” from TSMC: Nvidia’s monopoly cash flows give it the volume and money to secure its massive supply-chain advantage by buying priority amongst TSMC’s customers.

It of course, wants to keep all customers happy… but some will get much more soup than others.

This is probably a huge factor in keeping their advantage over their customers and competitors (but I repeat myself.) That is, TPUs and Trainium etc simply cannot acquire the necessary volume of chips at a competitive enough price-point to put a dent in Nvidia’s grip on the market. But the hyperscalers need all that compute NOW NOW NOW, so they have no choice but to turn around and begrudgingly pay Nvidia for that supply. Which puts more cash flow in Nvidia’s pocket, which buys them more soup, and on this loop continues.

children.author: retwakm4
children.textRawHtml:
The Hyperscalers are often working with a company like Broadcom (the elephant in the room on this topic) to design said chips. They don't usually have the amount of ASIC and Networking and Optics hardware expertise in house that would be required. See, for instance, Google's TPUs. Broadcom's hardware people are world class and some of the best paid in the business. It's the most elite hardware company in a lot of ways in terms of total comp for top engineers.

Google hires some hardware people to come up with general requirements for specialized stuff like ASICs, then sends those requirements to Broadcom to do the hard parts and negotiates big multi-billion dollar contracts with them. OpenAI did the same and contracted Broadcom after liking what they saw with the TPUs. There are several other Broadcom customers that I'm probably not at liberty to disclose.

But no, as far as GPU replacements are concerned, the Hyperscalers generally are not experienced enough in the specific types of hardware required to do this by themselves. It's very specialized and boutique high price work and more difficult than say, designing an ARM chip (something a company like Amazon or Google could probably handle in house).

In general though, yes, I agree. Hyperscalers are trying to reduce dependence on NVIDIA. Many are quite far along in their ASIC projects (Google especially, they are on their 8th generation TPU! Way past just being a small scale experiment by now.) and have large volumes of them running in place of NVIDIA chips and much more efficiently already.

Broadcom is fabless, and uses TSMC for these sorts of chips. They are mostly a boutique design "mercenary" firm for exactly this sort of specialized hardware for Hyperscaler customers and other clients that run significant amounts of infrastructure in house (so, think JP Morgan for instance). That's the core of their business, along with increasingly Infrastructure Software in the form of virtualization and mainframes and private and hybrid cloud (so some natural sales overlap there, just generally, "big companies that need specialized big data center hardware and software").

I remember that back in the 80s, when I was still deciding what I wanted to do when I grew up, there was a distinction between a "programmer" and a "systems analyst".

The systems analyst analyzed the problem that needed to be solved and designed a solution involving a computer, including system modules, inputs, outputs, etc.

The programmer, supposedly a lower paid profession, transformed that into Computer code. I remember someone telling me that wasn't the best choice and that I should become a "systems analyst". They wore the better suits.

My college even offered a shorter, cheaper degree for people who just wanted to be "programmers".

I think this distinction still survives in government labor statistics.

Perhaps we came full circle with LLMs partially killing the "programmer" job.

children.author: saltcured
children.textRawHtml:
In my opinion, a lot of that "no longer getting it" is because of the social/fashion trends that continually disrupt programming.

You don't forget CS concepts so easily, but all the syntactic tricks of new language variants and working set vocabulary of APIs, data formats, and frameworks keeps churning away from whatever you last had contacted in a real, hands-on way.

It is fascinating, wondering where this is going as programmers turn into their own middle managers on top of agents. Particularly, the school who claim that you don't really need to understand all the code and instead treat it like a black-box experiment. If this fad takes over the main stage, then everyone becomes one of those less technical managers.

But, in this new scenario, there is no human in the loop to inject judgement calls and "manage up" anymore. There is no programmer culture except the models and agents, which don't really have the same social connections to drive a programming culture. What will happen? A culture per agent product? Per enterprise client of the agent vendor? Per agent operator? Per codebase?

> Common among them is that they are often delay projects championing their pet idea, sometimes bringing negative value to the project.

Negative value to the project, perhaps; but if these "software architects" are kept around despite several rounds of this, it may be because they're providing positive value to the company, in terms of producing for the company a thing whose existence (no matter how flawed) serves as collateral for:

- the executive team, to show to investors, to convince them that they're acting strategically in the market; or

- the marketing team, to get breathless puff-piece articles written about the company, in places where dumb CTOs/CIOs who make IT buying decisions will read them. (Not necessarily to then buy the specific product that came out of that project — hopefully not, in fact! — but instead to remember the company itself the next time they're comparing vendors for something else);

- or the executive team again, this time to show to a potential acquirer, to convince the acquirer that their employees have a higher asset value for having a certain skill / experience with certain paradigms, that they gained working on this project.

Companies have spent collective billions (trillions?) of dollars on projects they know will go nowhere, just to be able to say they did a project that is made a certain way or does a certain thing or has certain certifications, and to have a shitty codebase they can pull out of their back pocket if needed to back that up. In all such cases, even if they need to present the product, the product will never be evaluated for its quality or for its fit-for-purpose-ness; so it doesn't matter that the project failed to produce something of quality or that is fit-for-purpose. It just matters that the project happened.

children.author: microtonal
children.textRawHtml:
The systems analyst analyzed the problem that needed to be solved and designed a solution involving a computer, including system modules, inputs, outputs, etc.

I think both definitions are still too narrow for what I do daily. I fully agree that we still need humans to decide what to build, how it should all fit together, etc.

But both definitions do not really take into account the huge social dimension of being a good (computer) engineer in a company. You have to translate requests from a wild variety of users into what this means for a system. You have to recognize and explain that what they need is not always what they think they need. You have to be able to say "no" to things. All these things are very hard for an LLM (reading humans, not literally following requests).

Then there are social aspects like building consensus within a project, building a user base of many people that are initially skeptical, using existing relations with people and other companies to slowly adopt what you are building, etc.

Programming used to be a large chunk of the work. I thoroughly enjoyed this aspect of the work when I was younger, but at some point I started enjoying system design and everything around it more. So in that sense, programming with LLMs is much nicer (though I still review every single line of code and often have to go through a couple of iterations because even Opus 5.5 often doesn't get it 'right' in the first take). But the remaining part of the work is extremely hard for an LLM to replace.

I’ve pulled that trick multiple times, normally successfully; some people appreciate such shenanigans.

A similar anecdote. There was once a bridge-building competition, with provided materials, and scores for it bearing different weight toy cars, for height and for length. Nowhere was it said the bridge had to bear any of the cars. Our group’s 15-metre long roll of tape bridge with four-pop-stick-A-frame supports, which scored three times as much as the next (… and we could have doubled its length), was unceremoniously disqualified for unspecified grounds, as I had expected. I pressed for a few days for the grounds (even suggesting the couple of not-unreasonable grounds I had thought of, such as that our team had schismed into two over the creative direction), but was not given them.

The unwritten rules about spirit can be applied capriciously.

I think ours was still the most popular bridge. And honestly one of the more realistic, just scaled for much smaller vehicles, a consistent 1:500 where most were an inconsistent 1:25 to 1:50. They were really good supports.

comments.author: fweimer
comments.textRawHtml:
Well, OpenOffice wouldn't print on Tuesdays:

“ What a fascinating bug!! My wife has complained that open office will never print on Tuesdays!?! Then she demonstrated it. Sure enough, won't print on Tuesday. Other applications print. I think this is the same bug. Here is my guess:

Print to a postscript file. Observe the line: %%CreationDate: (Tue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Change "Tue" to anything else: %%CreationDate: (XTue Mar 3 19:47:42 2009)

Save the file and it prints. Tools like evince work because they simply omit the "CreationDate" tag to begin with.

Now something odd happens when my cups script (I am using the Brother MFC420CN) copies the file to a temp file. Some of the code is rearranged, not sure how or why, but it uses a command called "file" to identify the file as "PostScript". This check would work on the original file you printed, but by the time it runs the check on the temp file, it misidentifies. Normally it would return:

   PostScript document text conforming at level 3.0
But there is another check that happens before the PostScript check. If it finds "Tue" at the fourth byte of the file, it identifies it as:

   Jan 22 14:32:44 MET 1991\011Erlang JAM file - version 4.2
So it's not a problem w/ openoffice.org, cups, or the brother printer drivers. It is a bug in the `file` utility, and documented at https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/file/+bug/248619. ”

https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/cupsys/+bug/255161...

But 5 steps later some tool looks at the image file and notices it's a valid zip file (creating files with multiple valid interpretations is something people have succeeded in doing it's not always so hard). It runs this check before the image check. The next step in the processing chain wants an image but it has been told it's dealing with a zip file. So it unzips the file to see if it contains an image. But it was a zip bomb. The server goes down.

Imagine a server allows you to upload images. It has a system designed for images only. It will behave unpredictably maybe even dangerously with another file. The server checks that the file ends with .jpg. it checks that the file is a valid jpeg. All clear. Upload allowed. But 5 steps later some tool looks at the image file and notices it's a valid zip file (creating files with multiple valid interpretations is something people have succeeded in doing it's not always so hard). It runs this check before the image check. The next step in the processing chain wants an image but it has been told it's dealing with a zip file. So it unzips the file to see if it contains an image. But it was a zip bomb. The server goes down.

That's not how a printer with a fax/modem works.

If the printer endpoint of the USB device receives a file that orders millions of pizzas, it will print the file (or print a PS error, or print the plaintext contents of the file), not order pizzas.

If the user mistakenly "prints" to the fax device, the file will be printed at the destination fax machine, at the number the user typed, not the number in the file, and it will print, not order pizzas (unless the pizzeria accepts fax orders, which would be a prank, not an attack).

children.author: kragen
children.textRawHtml:
Usually people advocate dependency cooldowns as a mitigation for supply-chain attacks, where you're depending on a module with a malicious maintainer, possibly a new one (perhaps one who stole the old maintainer's keys so they can pretend to be the old maintainer).

In that situation, how do you distinguish between "normal updates" (that you should let cool down) and "security advisories"? If all the hypothetical malicious maintainer has to do to get you to update is to publish a security advisory for their own package, wouldn't they just do that? It might even be a real advisory about a real security hole that they introduced, but claiming more versions are affected than actually are affected.

children.author: derefr
children.textRawHtml:
Why wouldn't a supply-chain attacker simply manipulate the project into producing a security advisory to get their exploit code pushed through inside a high-priority release?

I.e. get a puppet/co-conspirator to push vulnerable code; wait until that code gets released as v1.2.3; submit other vulnerable code; wait for that code to be merged and released as v1.2.4; then submit a vuln report for the vuln introduced in v1.2.3; and wait for v1.2.3 + v1.2.4 to be security-deprecated and v1.2.5 to be fast-released to replace them.

Now v1.2.5 exists and has your still-unknown 0day in it, while versions prior to v1.2.5 are deprecated. If devtools that had pinned v1.2.3 get forced "upward" to v1.2.5 despite the cooldown, you win.

children.author: dns_snek
children.textRawHtml:
I haven't seen anyone advocate against cooldowns because those are completely different problems.

How would removing cooldowns help you patch vulnerabilities? That would imply that your CI is configured to update dependencies, rebuild, and push them to production without human oversight?

That's obviously not the way to go, you must have human oversight and if you do then your humans should be alerted when one of your dependencies patches a security issue. At that point you review it, override the cooldown, and push it to production.
